noon at o'clock at the residence of
her parents, and seldom if ever in this
city have so many people gathered for
a last sad farewell to departed
friend. The old and young who had
met her so often in church and Sun
day school; her associates in school;
the wide circle of friends and acquint-
ances in the city; all came to pay
the tribute of their presence and their
tears. During the children's concert
and Sunday school in the morning at
the Presbyterian church, Of which she
was devoted member and regular
attendant, heavy cloud seemed to-
hang over the congregation, and as
they dispersed every one seemed to
think only of the great sorrow that
had fallen upon them. At the funeral
the many fearful eyes told more plain
ly than words the large place she held
in the hearts of those who knew her.,

Schmidt, VIM. Osborne, James Chap.
man, Louis Kruger, Chas. Willard and
Paul Barney, all members of the High.

row, and Messrs. Brett and Thomas.
with Miss Chesire as organist.

the noble character and beautiful life
of the deceased, of the words Of deep
regard and high esteem that came
from every side, especially from those.
who knew her best; and read a touch.
ing note from Prof. Bechdolt recount.
ing her peculiar graces of mind and
heart as he had learned them from
her school life. She graduated from
the High school only few days ago,
and was just stepping forth into life
that was full of hope and promise.
Her bright intellect, untiring indus
try, indomitable will and sunny dis
position always made her a leader.
Her commencement thesis, which her
last sickness prevented her from de-
livering, was about Historic Girls"
and it was Of especial significance
now for surely hers was nature that
makes heroines. Mr.. Corey spoke
briefly and earnestly Of the ''hope be-
yond' and of the comforting assurance
that the loved one departed had en-
tered into her eternal rest.


The procession from the house to
the cemetery was perhaps the longest
ever seen in Mankato. At the grave,

er has the death of one so young

words of sympathy for those be-
reaved.

mate, Schoolmate and companion, Luz

from among us, and her smile and

fore be it

the parents, brothers and sisters of

Editor Morning News: If it is fact that the smallpox was introduced into this city by the Spanish steamship Pinillos should there not be thorough investigation into the matter, with a view of ascertaining why the unsanitary condition of that vessel was not discovered by those who are entrusted safeguarding the port and city against the introduction of infectious or contagious diseases? The Pinillos was detained only twenty-four hours at quarantine, though she came direct from Havana to this port. Now, it is notorious that the former port is always more or less unhealthy, and it has been, and still is, customary to maintain a most rigid quarantine on sailing vessels from that latitude. W. J. THOMPSON, Savannah Pilot.

"This is no occasion for the exercise of your sarcastic powers, Mr. Martin," said the colonel severely. "It is to be hoped your civility was less a transparent sham than your present remarks."

"Pardon me, colonel," interposed Lieut. Lee, whose seat was near the window. "Here comes the gentleman himself."

Surely enough, a buggy drew up in front of the office, a bulky form slowly descended, and with much deliberation of manner Mr. Abrams, of Chicago, looked about him, then proceeded to tie his horse to a young maple at the edge of the walk. The orderly sprang forward:

"Against whose orders?" said the gentleman from Chicago, with slow and impressive movement, turning upon the trim soldier.

"The colonel's orders, sir. Even the officers can't leave their horses in front of headquarters, sir."

"My God! Here! This will never do!" fidgeted the colonel, springing to his feet. "Mr. Adjutant, send a man out here."

By this time, paying no attention to the orderly, the representative of The Palladium had reached the doorway and was brought face to face with the post commander:

"Col. Morris, I presume. I am the bearer of an order to you from department headquarters."

"Col. Morris, sir, at your service," replied the post commander with much suavity. "A letter, I presume. Walk in, Mr. Abrams. Take a chair, sir."

Several of the officers nearest the door had risen promptly, as though in readiness to receive with due honors the colonel's guest. Others slowly followed their example. Some remained seated and continued a low toned chat. All gradually resumed their seats, and, while some with evident curiosity studied the appearance of the stranger, Brodie and Lee looked at him with eyes that plainly spoke their resentment, while Hearn's hands were clinched and his lips compressed. No word was spoken to the new arrival, however. He, with entire indifference of manner as to all the rest, fixed his gaze upon the commanding officer, who rapidly read. "I am greatly pleased to welcome you, Mr. Abrams," he said, extending to his hand with much apparent cordiality of manner. "This, while by no means necessary, of course adds to the readiness with which we open our doors to you. Had I known you were here on the purpose of visiting the post in the interests of your paper, I should have found means to welcome you before, and am only sorry you did not make your presence known to me."

Maj. Kenyon had risen as the colonel was speaking, and now in low tone and with much respect of manner accosted him:

"By your leave, colonel, if there is nothing further in the way of business, may I request your permission to retire?"

For a moment no one among the little group seemed to find anything to say; it was Mr. Lee who gave the first expression to personal opinion. He burst out into a fit of laughter.

"I'm blessed if I can see anything to laugh about in this affair, Mr. Lee."

Princeton, N. J., Sept 20.—Dr. W. H. Green, moderator of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church, in his opening sermon to the students of Princeton Theological Seminary this morning, preached on the subject. The Word of God in referring to the higher critics, and the positions taken by them he said:

The Bible has been assailed by Biblical criticism. Critical attacks upon the Bible are no new thing. The new thing is that prominent workers in the Church accept their views. Second, we can acknowledge the critics' position. Denying that Moses wrote the Pentateuch does not affect the inspiration of the Pentateuch. Our faith will be safe. The contents will remain the same.
